newsitem.title: NORWAY: US hull insurers face losses in '96, '97 - industry.
newsitem.headline: US hull insurers face losses in '96, '97 - industry.

text.p: U.S. ship insurance companies will make losses in 1996 and 1997 because of plummeting premium rates, the American Institute of Marine Underwriters (AIMU) said on Tuesday.

John Hickey, president of the American Hull Insurance Syndicate and the AIMU's hull spokesman, told Reuters at a conference in Oslo that insurance rates were in freefall because there were too many competitors in the multi-billion dollar market.
"1996 is already a loss underwriting year, although some people haven't worked it out yet, and 1997 will be worse," said Hickey.

He predicted that in 1997 the combination of expenses and claims costs (combined ratio) would reach around 110 percent of premiums earned in. That means a loss to the market which had a combined ratio of 76.72 percent in 1995.

"Rate falls have been significant. There have been reductions and reductions and reductions. The only thing that has not cracked yet is deductibles. It looks like we are going to get sicker before we get better," said Hickey.

The hull market managed to return to profitable insurance rating in 1992, after a series of major shipping losses between 1989 and 1991 on low-rated policies pushed combined ratios as high as 200 percent and forced several insurers to give up marine underwriting altogether.

But a couple of recent years of profit have attracted new insurance capacity to the market, and increased competition combined with the lack of a major insured loss allowed brokers to push prices down.
Oil and energy insurers were now facing a similar scenario, said Pete Connors of insurance giant American International Group (AIG).
"The offshore energy market is headed in the same direction as hull. Rates started softening in 1995 and this continued in 1996," added Connors.
"The major oil companies are keeping larger retentions, yet there is $2.8 billion capacity in the oil insurance market chasing too few premium dollars," he added.

Connors pointed out that low rates meant insurers were not building up a bank of money to pay for major energy insurance losses if they came. "And it's not a case of if they come, it's when," he said.
Total marine net premiums for the U.S. marine insurance market were $1.22 billion in 1995, up from $1.21 billion in 1994.
The combined ratio for all lines improved to 91.2 percent from 93.5 percent the previous year. The combined ratio for hull insurance fell to 76.7 percent from 82.5 percent in 1994.
The AIMU pointed out that a couple of years ago, even a 100 percent ratio would have been welcomed.
